fatal_errors: The proposed intervention changes oxygen partial pressure, whereas the governing comparison was as-printed versus 750°C/50 h precipitation-aged material under isothermal oxidation.
The starting state is incorrectly described as already containing ordered strengthening precipitates; the as-printed baseline was single-fcc and lacked the aged L12/L21 nanoprecipitate population.

The hypothesis replaces oxidation-scale growth with creep-induced catastrophic fracture, although creep loading, interfacial cracking, and catastrophic mechanical failure were not established outcomes of the target study.

It omits the central protective mechanism: formation of a continuous Cr-rich, primarily Cr2O3, barrier and delayed barrier establishment in the aged state due to Cr-depleted precipitates and additional interfaces.
The cited evidence concerns creep of a different high-entropy superalloy and supports precipitate strengthening and rafting, not oxygen-assisted interfacial oxidation or cracking in this alloy.
explanation: The response offers a testable oxidizing-versus-inert creep experiment, but it does not reconstruct the studied degradation mechanism or controlled comparison. The target behavior was oxidation of as-printed and precipitation-aged specimens from 600–1200°C for up to 96 h. Aging generated L12/L21 precipitates, locally depleted Cr, and added possible short-circuit oxygen paths, causing greater mass gain and delayed formation of an equally protective Cr2O3 layer. Both states nevertheless retained similar activation energies and Cr2O3-mediated protection. The generated hypothesis instead assumes precipitates in the baseline, focuses on oxide-induced misfit strain and catastrophic creep cracking at about 982°C, and uses an inert atmosphere as its baseline. Its experiment could distinguish atmosphere-dependent mechanical degradation, but it does not directly isolate the precipitation/Cr-distribution mechanism, and its broad null-result falsification rule does not test the asserted causal chain between interfacial oxidation, misfit stress, creep, and fracture.
